claim: Tissue-clearing and labeling techniques have revolutionized brain-wide imaging and analysis.
source: Tissue-clearing and labeling techniques have revolutionized brain-wide imaging and analysis, yet their application to clinical formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks remains challenging.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of neuroscience and tissue imaging.

claim: Application of tissue-clearing and labeling techniques to clinical FFPE blocks remains challenging.
source: Tissue-clearing and labeling techniques have revolutionized brain-wide imaging and analysis, yet their application to clinical formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks remains challenging.
evidence: This is supported by the context of the study and references to previous limitations in the field.

claim: HIF-Clear is a novel method for efficiently clearing and labeling centimeter-thick FFPE specimens using elevated temperature and concentrated detergents.
source: We introduce HIF-Clear, a novel method for efficiently clearing and labeling centimeter-thick FFPE specimens using elevated temperature and concentrated detergents.
evidence: This is the primary methodological claim of the manuscript, describing the new technique developed by the authors.

claim: HIF-Clear with multi-round immunolabeling reveals neuron circuitry regulating multiple neurotransmitter systems in a whole FFPE mouse brain.
source: HIF-Clear with multi-round immunolabeling reveals neuron circuitry regulating multiple neurotransmitter systems in a whole FFPE mouse brain and is able to be used as the evaluation of disease treatment efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing six-round immunolabeling of different neuronal markers in the manuscript.

claim: HIF-Clear can be used for evaluation of disease treatment efficiency.
source: HIF-Clear with multi-round immunolabeling reveals neuron circuitry regulating multiple neurotransmitter systems in a whole FFPE mouse brain and is able to be used as the evaluation of disease treatment efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the TBI mouse model experiments showing therapeutic effects of different treatments.

claim: HIF-Clear supports expansion microscopy.
source: HIF-Clear also supports expansion microscopy and can be performed on a non-sectioned 15-year-old FFPE specimen, as well as a 3-month formalin-fixed mouse brain.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8 showing expansion microscopy results.

claim: HIF-Clear can be performed on a non-sectioned 15-year-old FFPE specimen.
source: HIF-Clear also supports expansion microscopy and can be performed on a non-sectioned 15-year-old FFPE specimen, as well as a 3-month formalin-fixed mouse brain.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C-E showing clear dopaminergic neuron clusters in a 15-year-old FFPE specimen.

claim: HIF-Clear can be performed on a 3-month formalin-fixed mouse brain.
source: HIF-Clear also supports expansion microscopy and can be performed on a non-sectioned 15-year-old FFPE specimen, as well as a 3-month formalin-fixed mouse brain.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 showing TH labeling in 3-month fixed specimens.

claim: HIF-Clear represents a feasible approach for researching archived FFPE specimens for future neuroscientific and 3D neuropathological analyses.
source: Thus, HIF-Clear represents a feasible approach for researching archived FFPE specimens for future neuroscientific and 3D neuropathological analyses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various experimental demonstrations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Clinical brain tissues play a critical role in unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying neurological diseases and facilitating the development of effective treatments.
source: Clinical brain tissues play a critical role in unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying neurological diseases and facilitating the development of effective treatments (Rajput and Rajput, 2015; Hernandez-Ronquillo et al., 2020; Latimer et al., 2023), and also represent an invaluable resource for retrospective studies on rare diseases or conditions with long-term outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clinical brain tissues represent an invaluable resource for retrospective studies on rare diseases or conditions with long-term outcomes.
source: Clinical brain tissues play a critical role in unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying neurological diseases and facilitating the development of effective treatments (Rajput and Rajput, 2015; Hernandez-Ronquillo et al., 2020; Latimer et al., 2023), and also represent an invaluable resource for retrospective studies on rare diseases or conditions with long-term outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Talari and Goyal, 2020 and general knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of archived clinical specimens are stored in the form of FFPE blocks.
source: Currently, the majority of archived clinical specimens are stored in the form of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks.
evidence: This is established knowledge in clinical pathology.

claim: Advanced molecular analysis tools such as chromatin immunoprecipitation, DNA/RNA sequencing, and Luminex assays have been performed on FFPE specimens.
source: Advanced molecular analysis tools—such as chromatin immunoprecipitation, DNA/RNA sequencing, and Luminex assays—have been performed on FFPE specimens to enable comprehensive analysis from genomic, transcriptional, and proteomic perspectives (Latimer et al., 2023; Jacobsen et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Image-based qualification and quantification of FFPE samples remain limited to performing chemical staining and immunohistochemistry on thin sections.
source: However, image-based qualification and quantification of FFPE samples remain limited to performing chemical staining and immunohistochemistry on thin sections.
evidence: This describes the current state of the field and the limitation that the study aims to address.

claim: Whole-slide imaging enables unbiased analyses of entire tissue sections.
source: Although whole-slide imaging enables unbiased analyses of entire tissue sections (Latimer et al., 2023; Fraggetta et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2021), its two-dimensional (2D) nature cannot provide the 3D information required for accurate quantification.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The 2D nature of whole-slide imaging cannot provide the 3D information required for accurate quantification.
source: Although whole-slide imaging enables unbiased analyses of entire tissue sections (Latimer et al., 2023; Fraggetta et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2020; Patel et al., 2021), its two-dimensional (2D) nature cannot provide the 3D information required for accurate quantification.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the inherent limitations of 2D imaging techniques.

claim: 3D quantification in neurobiological contexts is crucial for evaluating neuronal damage and neuroprotection, including neuronal cell counts and the extent of necrosis.
source: Such quantification in neurobiological contexts is crucial for evaluating neuronal damage and neuroprotection, including neuronal cell counts and the extent of necrosis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in neuroscience research.

claim: 2D-based techniques fail to reveal structural changes within target tissues.
source: Moreover, such 2D-based techniques also fail to reveal structural changes within target tissues.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of 2D imaging.

claim: Tissue-clearing protocols in combination with deep-tissue immunolabeling and optical sectioning microscopy techniques represent powerful tools for collecting 3D information at a subcellular resolution from centimeter-scale specimens.
source: Tissue-clearing protocols (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Ueda et al., 2020; Gómez-Gaviro et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2021) in combination with deep-tissue immunolabeling (Yun et al., 2019; Susaki et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2023) and optical sectioning microscopy techniques (Conchello and Lichtman, 2005; Dodt et al., 2007; Reynaud et al., 2008) represent powerful tools for collecting 3D information at a subcellular resolution from centimeter-scale specimens.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Tissue-clearing techniques render biological tissues transparent by removing components that induce refraction index mismatching.
source: Tissue-clearing techniques render biological tissues transparent by removing components that induce refraction index mismatching, which is mainly attributable to two factors, that is, light absorption due to pigments or biological chromophores and light scattering mainly caused by lipids (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature explaining the mechanism of tissue clearing.

claim: Refraction index mismatching is mainly attributable to light absorption due to pigments or biological chromophores and light scattering mainly caused by lipids.
source: Tissue-clearing techniques render biological tissues transparent by removing components that induce refraction index mismatching, which is mainly attributable to two factors, that is, light absorption due to pigments or biological chromophores and light scattering mainly caused by lipids (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In current tissue-clearing protocols, samples are fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for ~24 hr before undergoing delipidation steps.
source: In current tissue-clearing protocols, samples are fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for ~24 hr before undergoing delipidation steps that involve solvents (Ertürk et al., 2012; Renier et al., 2014; Jing et al., 2018), aqueous solutions with denaturing reagents or detergents (Hama et al., 2011; Susaki et al., 2014; Hama et al., 2015; Tainaka et al., 2018), or protection with chemicals that create crosslinks to withstand harsh electrophoretic delipidation (Chung et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2015; Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing current tissue-clearing protocols.

claim: Current tissue-clearing protocols now enable imaging of whole-rodent bodies and even entire human organs at the cellular or subcellular level.
source: Such protocols now enable imaging of whole-rodent bodies (Cai et al., 2019; Mai et al., 2024) and even entire human organs at the cellular or subcellular level (Zhao et al., 2020), facilitating detailed and comprehensive analyses of intact biological systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FFPE specimens have not reaped the benefits of advanced tissue-clearing techniques.
source: However, FFPE specimens have not reaped the benefits of these advanced techniques.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of limited success with previous approaches.

claim: Tissue-clearing approaches such as CUBIC, iDISCO, CLARITY, and passive SDS treatment applied to FFPE specimens have only yielded immunolabeling depths of 1–2 mm.
source: For instance, although tissue-clearing approaches such as CUBIC, iDISCO, CLARITY, and passive Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) treatment have been applied previously to FFPE specimens (Chen et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2014; Lai et al., 2018; Nojima et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2018), they have only yielded immunolabeling depths of 1–2 mm, underscoring the need for a procedure tailored to FFPE samples in order to achieve centimeter-scale tissue clearing and labeling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies showing limited penetration depth.

claim: Successful immunohistochemistry of FFPE tissue sections requires antigen retrieval to restore target conformation and expose masked epitopes.
source: First, successful immunohistochemistry of FFPE tissue sections requires antigen retrieval to restore target conformation and expose masked epitopes (Shi et al., 2001; Thavarajah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on antigen retrieval methods.

claim: Despite xylene treatment during paraffin processing and dewaxing protocols removing a substantial proportion of FFPE tissue lipids, certain phospholipids persist within the lipid bilayer.
source: Secondly, despite xylene treatment during paraffin processing and dewaxing protocols removing a substantial proportion of FFPE tissue lipids, certain phospholipids persist within the lipid bilayer, impeding antibody penetration and maintaining opacity (Nojima et al., 2017; Denti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Residual phospholipids in FFPE tissues impede antibody penetration and maintain opacity.
source: Secondly, despite xylene treatment during paraffin processing and dewaxing protocols removing a substantial proportion of FFPE tissue lipids, certain phospholipids persist within the lipid bilayer, impeding antibody penetration and maintaining opacity (Nojima et al., 2017; Denti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SDS is a detergent commonly used for lipid removal in tissue-clearing methods.
source: SDS is a detergent commonly used for lipid removal in tissue-clearing methods.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of tissue clearing.

claim: SDS is known as an antigen retrieval agent and has been used to enhance immunolabeling signals in cells, cryosections, formalin-fixed human brains, and epithelia of the pancreas, liver, and lung.
source: It is also known as an antigen retrieval agent and has been used to enhance immunolabeling signals in cells (Robinson and Vandré, 2001), cryosections (Brown et al., 1996), formalin-fixed human brains (Woelfle et al., 2023), and epithelia of the pancreas, liver, and lung (Messal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: FLASH-processed samples showed weak tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) signal.
source: We observed that both FLASH-processed and SDS-electrophoresed samples showed weak tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, a marker of dopaminergic neurons) signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: SDS-electrophoresed samples showed weak tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) signal.
source: We observed that both FLASH-processed and SDS-electrophoresed samples showed weak tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, a marker of dopaminergic neurons) signal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: FLASH-processed samples had almost no signal of NeuN.
source: Additionally, we noticed that the FLASH-processed samples had almost no signal of NeuN (a marker of neuronal nuclei, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, left), and exhibited strong nonspecific background noise (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: FLASH-processed samples exhibited strong nonspecific background noise.
source: Additionally, we noticed that the FLASH-processed samples had almost no signal of NeuN (a marker of neuronal nuclei, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, left), and exhibited strong nonspecific background noise (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, left).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The presence of background noise is considered an indicator of inadequate antigen retrieval.
source: The presence of this background noise is considered an indicator of inadequate antigen retrieval (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SDS-electrophoresed samples possessed weak TH-positive signal and strong nonspecific labeling.
source: We also observed that the SDS-electrophoresed sample only possessed weak TH-positive signal, as well as strong nonspecific labeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, right), with this latter considered an indicator of inadequate antigen retrieval (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Insufficient antigen retrieval using SDS approaches is likely due to low-temperature experimental conditions.
source: These results imply insufficient antigen retrieval using the SDS approaches, likely due to the low-temperature experimental conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and comparison with higher temperature methods.

claim: Shi et al. published a heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER) method utilizing a temperature of 100°C in 1991.
source: In 1991, Shi et al. published a heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER) method utilizing a temperature of 100°C (Shi et al., 1991), which now represents the most broad-spectrum antigen retrieval protocol for FFPE tissue sections.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original publication.

claim: HIER at 100°C represents the most broad-spectrum antigen retrieval protocol for FFPE tissue sections.
source: In 1991, Shi et al. published a heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER) method utilizing a temperature of 100°C (Shi et al., 1991), which now represents the most broad-spectrum antigen retrieval protocol for FFPE tissue sections.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of histopathology.

claim: Superheating (temperatures >100°C) in pressure cookers has been reported to enhance immunohistochemistry signal intensity and stability.
source: Superheating (i.e., temperatures >100°C) in pressure cookers has been reported to enhance immunohistochemistry signal intensity and stability (Norton et al., 1994; Taylor et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Heating with classical antigen retrieval citrate buffer at 121°C for 10 min in a pressure cooker resulted in weak immunostaining signals of NeuN and SMI312 in the middle of a 2-mm-thick FFPE mouse brain block.
source: However, heating with a classical antigen retrieval citrate buffer (10 mM sodium citrate, pH 6.0) at 121°C for 10 min in a pressure cooker, a condition appropriate for routine FFPE sections, only resulted in weak immunostaining signals of NeuN and SMI312 (a pan-neurofilament marker) in the middle of a 2-mm-thick FFPE mouse brain block (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, middle column).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Dewaxed and rehydrated FFPE specimens still have residual phospholipids that prevent antibody penetration.
source: Since dewaxed and rehydrated FFPE specimens still have residual phospholipids that prevent antibody penetration (Nojima et al., 2017; Denti et al., 2020), we added 1% SDS into the citrate buffer to increase the delipidation capability of the HIER approach and found that NeuN and SMI312 signals were significantly enhanced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, right).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Adding 1% SDS into the citrate buffer significantly enhanced NeuN and SMI312 signals.
source: Since dewaxed and rehydrated FFPE specimens still have residual phospholipids that prevent antibody penetration (Nojima et al., 2017; Denti et al., 2020), we added 1% SDS into the citrate buffer to increase the delipidation capability of the HIER approach and found that NeuN and SMI312 signals were significantly enhanced (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Deploying SDS at high temperatures resulted in tissue expansion and fragility.
source: However, deploying SDS at such high temperatures also resulted in tissue expansion and fragility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, gross view), prompting us to search for a detergent condition that could achieve sufficient delipidation while retaining tissue integrity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NaC and CHAPS have higher critical micelle concentrations and form smaller micelles than SDS.
source: NaC and CHAPS have higher critical micelle concentrations and form smaller micelles than SDS, and both have been reported as being more efficient than SDS with respect to active electrophoretic delipidation (Na et al., 2022) and passive delipidation (Zhao et al., 2020), respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about detergent properties.

claim: NaC has been reported as being more efficient than SDS with respect to active electrophoretic delipidation.
source: NaC and CHAPS have higher critical micelle concentrations and form smaller micelles than SDS, and both have been reported as being more efficient than SDS with respect to active electrophoretic delipidation (Na et al., 2022) and passive delipidation (Zhao et al., 2020), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CHAPS has been reported as being more efficient than SDS with respect to passive delipidation.
source: NaC and CHAPS have higher critical micelle concentrations and form smaller micelles than SDS, and both have been reported as being more efficient than SDS with respect to active electrophoretic delipidation (Na et al., 2022) and passive delipidation (Zhao et al., 2020), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The FFPE group without HIER exhibited a higher DiD signal intensity than the PFA-SDS group but lower than that of the undelipidated group.
source: The FFPE group without HIER exhibited a higher DiD signal intensity than the PFA-SDS group but lower than that of the undelipidated group, supporting partial lipid removal during the paraffin processing and dewaxing process.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Paraffin processing and dewaxing process results in partial lipid removal.
source: The FFPE group without HIER exhibited a higher DiD signal intensity than the PFA-SDS group but lower than that of the undelipidated group, supporting partial lipid removal during the paraffin processing and dewaxing process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the DiD signal intensity data.

claim: Only the 1% Tween 20 condition presented significantly lower lipid content compared to the FFPE without HIER group (p-value=0.0035).
source: Among all of the test groups subjected to varied heated detergent conditions, only the 1% Tween 20 condition presented significantly lower lipid content compared to the FFPE without HIER group (p-value=0.0035), achieving the same level of delipidation as the PFA-SDS group (p-value=0.999) (Figure 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The 1% Tween 20 condition achieved the same level of delipidation as the PFA-SDS group (p-value=0.999).
source: Among all of the test groups subjected to varied heated detergent conditions, only the 1% Tween 20 condition presented significantly lower lipid content compared to the FFPE without HIER group (p-value=0.0035), achieving the same level of delipidation as the PFA-SDS group (p-value=0.999) (Figure 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The 1% Tween 20 group displayed the sharpest and clearest neuronal nuclei and axon bundles with a high signal-to-background ratio.
source: We found that the 1% Tween 20 group displayed the sharpest and clearest neuronal nuclei and axon bundles with a high signal-to-background ratio, indicating both successful delipidation and antigen retrieval (Figure 1B, panel 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For the 1% Triton X-100, 1% NaC, and 1% CHAPS groups, the fluorescence intensity of neuronal nuclei was even lower than the background signal.
source: Interestingly, for the 1% Triton X-100, 1% NaC, and 1% CHAPS groups, the fluorescence intensity of neuronal nuclei was even lower than the background signal, implying that heating these detergents might hinder nuclear epitopes (Figure 1B, panels 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Heating Triton X-100, NaC, and CHAPS might hinder nuclear epitopes.
source: Interestingly, for the 1% Triton X-100, 1% NaC, and 1% CHAPS groups, the fluorescence intensity of neuronal nuclei was even lower than the background signal, implying that heating these detergents might hinder nuclear epitopes (Figure 1B, panels 3–5).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The 1% Tween 20 group retained good sample integrity without apparent changes in size or color.
source: We also examined the gross appearance of each group upon heating, which confirmed that the 1% Tween 20 group retained good sample integrity without apparent changes in size or color (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 1% Tween 20 in citrate buffer with heating in a pressure cooker at 121°C for 10 min is employed as the critical step of the HIF-Clear pipeline for delipidation and antigen retrieval of centimeter-scale FFPE specimens.
source: Therefore, we employed 1% Tween 20 in citrate buffer with heating in a pressure cooker at 121°C for 10 min as the critical step of our HIF-Clear pipeline for delipidation and antigen retrieval of centimeter-scale FFPE specimens.
evidence: This is the key methodological conclusion drawn from the optimization experiments.

claim: When working on a large sample, the dewaxing time should be increased to avoid opacity caused by residual wax due to insufficient dewaxing.
source: It is important to note that when working on a large sample, the dewaxing time should be increased to avoid opacity caused by residual wax due to insufficient dewaxing.
evidence: This is a practical recommendation based on experimental observations.

claim: Opacity can be eliminated through repeated dehydration and dewaxing steps.
source: Opacity can be eliminated through repeated dehydration and dewaxing steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b), with extended dewaxing times or repeated dewaxing steps not affecting tissue structure or antigenicity (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Extended dewaxing times or repeated dewaxing steps do not affect tissue structure or antigenicity.
source: Opacity can be eliminated through repeated dehydration and dewaxing steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b), with extended dewaxing times or repeated dewaxing steps not affecting tissue structure or antigenicity (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: A typical dewaxing timeframe for paraffin sections of less than 20 µm thickness is ~20 min.
source: A typical dewaxing timeframe for paraffin sections of less than 20 µm thickness is ~20 min, with complete dewaxing of an entire mouse brain or similarly sized sample achievable within 24 hr (see 'Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and practical experience.

claim: Complete dewaxing of an entire mouse brain or similarly sized sample is achievable within 24 hr.
source: A typical dewaxing timeframe for paraffin sections of less than 20 µm thickness is ~20 min, with complete dewaxing of an entire mouse brain or similarly sized sample achievable within 24 hr (see 'Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and practical experience.

claim: Both the FFPE-HIF-Clear-processed and PFA-SDS-treated mouse brain samples displayed significantly lower CARS signals compared to a dewaxed FFPE mouse brain.
source: In contrast to a dewaxed FFPE mouse brain (Figure 1D, left) for which we observed CARS signals from axon bundles, thus indicating the presence of myelinated lipids, both the FFPE-HIF-Clear-processed and PFA-SDS-treated mouse brain samples displayed significantly lower CARS signals (Figure 1E, middle and right, respectively; quantification in Figure 1F), confirming removal of myelinated lipids.
evidence: This is supported by CARS imaging data shown in Figure 1E and quantification in Figure 1F.

claim: HIF-Clear confirms removal of myelinated lipids from FFPE mouse brains.
source: In contrast to a dewaxed FFPE mouse brain (Figure 1D, left) for which we observed CARS signals from axon bundles, thus indicating the presence of myelinated lipids, both the FFPE-HIF-Clear-processed and PFA-SDS-treated mouse brain samples displayed significantly lower CARS signals (Figure 1E, middle and right, respectively; quantification in Figure 1F), confirming removal of myelinated lipids.
evidence: This is supported by CARS imaging data shown in Figure 1E and quantification in Figure 1F.

claim: Previous studies have confirmed that transcriptomic and proteomic data are equally preserved in FFPE sections and fresh-frozen sections.
source: Previous studies have confirmed that transcriptomic and proteomic data are equally preserved in FFPE sections and fresh-frozen sections.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: Patterns of anti-TH antibody labeling in FFPE-HIF-Clear-processed mouse brains show consistent distributions of dopaminergic neurons in key tissue regions.
source: We observed consistent distributions of dopaminergic neurons in key tissue regions, including the striatum, nigrostriatal fiber tracts, substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area, pontine reticular nucleus, and lateral reticular nucleus, aligning with the findings of a prior study (Susaki et al., 2020; Figure 2A, left) and matching results from Allen Brain Atlas registration (Claudi et al., 2020; Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The volume of each brain region between the left and right hemispheres revealed minimal sample distortion.
source: Furthermore, we compared the volume of each brain region between the left and right hemispheres, which revealed minimal sample distortion (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HIF-Clear revealed clear clusters of dopaminergic neurons at a cellular resolution in a 15-year-old FFPE specimen.
source: Our investigation extended to a 2-mm-thick mouse brain that had been preserved in an FFPE block for 15 y. By applying HIF-Clear, we unveiled clear clusters of dopaminergic neurons at a cellular resolution in that specimen (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HIF-Clear is feasible for long-term stored FFPE blocks without the need for sectioning.
source: These results confirm the feasibility of deploying HIF-Clear for long-term stored FFPE blocks, even without the need for sectioning, enabling effective retrieval of information on spatial biomarkers comparable to that obtained from freshly fixed samples.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with the 15-year-old specimen.

claim: Long-term fixed specimens exhibited reduced TH intensity and S/N ratio.
source: Although the long-term fixed specimens exhibited reduced TH intensity and S/N ratio, the major dopaminergic regions were labeled, and magnified images revealed clear details of cell bodies and neuronal fibers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HIF-Clear has the potential to be applied to long-term fixed specimens.
source: These results suggest that HIF-Clear has the potential to be applied to long-term fixed specimens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with 3-month fixed specimens.

claim: Post-staining fixation is required to maintain signals in a centimeter-sized sample.
source: However, based on our preliminary experiments, we found that post-staining fixation is required to maintain signals in a centimeter-sized sample (i.e., a whole mouse brain) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and the post-fixed antibodies cannot be completely stripped using SDS-based stripping protocols (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Post-fixed antibodies cannot be completely stripped using SDS-based stripping protocols.
source: However, based on our preliminary experiments, we found that post-staining fixation is required to maintain signals in a centimeter-sized sample (i.e., a whole mouse brain) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and the post-fixed antibodies cannot be completely stripped using SDS-based stripping protocols (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fixation after staining hindered subsequent rounds of staining, although this impediment could be overcome by traditional heat-induced epitope retrieval.
source: We also observed that fixation after staining hindered subsequent rounds of staining, although this impediment could be overcome by traditional heat-induced epitope retrieval (referred to hereafter as classical HIER to avoid confusion with the aforementioned optimized antigen retrieval protocol) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: HIF-Clear+ includes a multi-round immunolabeling protocol utilizing photobleaching and classical HIER.
source: To overcome the difficulty of antibody stripping due to post-fixation, which is required for centimeter-sized specimens, we developed HIF-Clear+ to include a multi-round immunolabeling protocol utilizing photobleaching and classical HIER (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the HIF-Clear+ protocol.

claim: Overnight bleaching is sufficient for tissue samples of <500 μm thickness.
source: The selected duration of bleaching is dependent on sample thickness; overnight bleaching is sufficient for tissue samples of <500 μm thickness, whereas ~72 hr are required for thicker samples such as whole mouse brains (a thickness of 0.8–1 cm).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and practical experience.

claim: ~72 hr of bleaching are required for thicker samples such as whole mouse brains (a thickness of 0.8–1 cm).
source: The selected duration of bleaching is dependent on sample thickness; overnight bleaching is sufficient for tissue samples of <500 μm thickness, whereas ~72 hr are required for thicker samples such as whole mouse brains (a thickness of 0.8–1 cm).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and practical experience.

claim: The brain shape and structural integrity remained after four rounds of immunolabeling.
source: The brain shape and structural integrity remained after four rounds of immunolabeling, and there is no cross-reactivity in subsequent rounds of immunostaining following bleaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: There is no cross-reactivity in subsequent rounds of immunostaining following bleaching.
source: The brain shape and structural integrity remained after four rounds of immunolabeling, and there is no cross-reactivity in subsequent rounds of immunostaining following bleaching (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: A six-round immunolabeling procedure for TH, TPH2, calbindin, PV, ChAT, and SMI312 was performed on one intact FFPE mouse brain.
source: To explore the potential of revealing multiple neuronal circuitry in the whole FFPE mouse brain using HIF-Clear+, we performed a six-round immunolabeling procedure for TH, tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (TPH2), calbindin, parvalbumin (PV), choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), and SMI312, respectively, on one intact FFPE mouse brain (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: HIF-Clear+ demonstrates the ability to reveal the spatial distribution of different neuronal markers.
source: Image datasets from each immunolabeling round were combined into a single multichannel image (Figure 5A and Figure 4—video 1), with lectin-labeled blood vessels deployed as a reference channel using Elastix (Klein et al., 2010), demonstrating the ability of HIF-Clear+ to reveal the spatial distribution of different neuronal markers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.
